query: For transition-metal catalysts, formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis explaining what governs catalytic activity, selectivity, or durability and why. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: For Pd@PdAg nanocrystals used in ethanol oxidation electrocatalysis, reducing the surface strain from approximately 2.1% to 0.3% will downshift the d-band center of Pd and Ag atoms, thereby weakening the binding of poisoning intermediates (e.g., *CH3CO) and enhancing both selectivity and durability relative to catalysts with higher strain.
generation.material_initial_state: Pd@PdAg nanocrystals synthesized with uniform composition and similar exposed facets but exhibiting a higher surface strain (~2.1%), as typically observed in icosahedral morphologies.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled synthesis modifications (such as using template selection or thermal treatments) to produce a set of Pd@PdAg nanocrystals that display a reduced surface strain (~0.3%), preferably with a {111} truncated bi-pyramid morphology.
generation.conditions: Conduct ethanol oxidation electrocatalytic tests under identical conditions (same electrolyte, temperature, applied potential, catalyst loading, and cell configuration) for both high-strain (baseline) and low-strain nanocrystals.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of surface strain, which alters the d-band center position of the surface Pd and Ag atoms.
generation.mechanism: Lower surface strain in the catalyst reduces the d-band center energy, which in turn weakens the adsorption energy of key intermediates (notably the *CH3CO species) that can poison the active sites. This facilitates faster desorption of intermediates, leading to enhanced selective oxidation kinetics and improved catalyst durability over multiple cycles.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanocrystals with ~0.3% surface strain will demonstrate higher ethanol oxidation activity, improved selectivity towards the desired product (e.g., the unsaturated alcohol) and increased operational durability, evidenced by lower overpotentials and more favorable Tafel slopes compared to the ~2.1% strained baseline.
generation.baseline: Catalysts of identical composition and morphology but with ~2.1% surface strain (e.g., Pd@PdAg icosahedra) that show relatively lower selectivity and stability in ethanol oxidation electrocatalysis.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for Pd@PdAg nanocatalysts in ethanol oxidation reactions under acidic or near-neutral conditions at ambient temperature, where surface strain is the dominant factor influencing the d-band center. Deviations might be observed if particle size effects or additional support interactions become significant.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative impact of strain on the precise shift of the d-band center may vary with particle size distribution and minor compositional inhomogeneities. There is also potential coupling with other factors (e.g., slight variations in surface roughness) that could influence the catalytic performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of Pd@PdAg nanocrystals with identical chemical compositions and overall morphologies but differing exclusively in measured surface strain (~0.3% vs. ~2.1%). Perform identical ethanol oxidation tests (via cyclic voltammetry, chronoamperometry) and use spectroscopic techniques (XPS/UPS) to ascertain the d-band center position. Compare product selectivity, overpotential values, Tafel slopes, and durability metrics between the two catalyst sets.
measurements: Surface strain quantification using transmission electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction.
Electrochemical measurements: cyclic voltammetry, Tafel analysis, chronoamperometry for durability.
Product distribution analysis using chromatographic methods.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the lower strain (~0.3%) Pd@PdAg nanocrystals do not exhibit a measurable downshift in the d-band center, or if there are no statistically significant improvements in catalytic activity, selectivity, and durability compared to the higher strain (~2.1%) baseline, then the hypothesis that reduced surface strain governs enhanced performance will be falsified.

The proposed HEzymes contain five transition metals with similar atomic radii, which frequently serve as the catalytic active sites of redox nanozymes, including manganese, iron, cobalt, nickel, and copper.[ ,  ] DFT calculations offer insight into the extraordinary POD‐like activity of the HEzymes. The strong interactions among the d electrons of the elements in the HEA NPs optimize the electronic distribution around the EFof the bulk material, which enhances the adsorption of intermediates at the surface‐active sites while increasing the efficiency of electron transfer during the catalytic process, thereby enhancing the performance of the nanocatalyst. As a proof of concept, the HEsymes were used as biosensors and in biomedicine. In addition to guaranteeing both selectivity and accuracy of the colorimetric platform for the target, the HEzymes also achieved efficient elimination of multidrug‐resistant bacteria and biofilm eradication by triggering ROS outbreaks. AbstractThe strain effect is a critical knob to tune the catalytic performance and has received unprecedented research interest recently. However, it is difficult to distinguish the strain effect from the synergistic effect, especially in alloyed catalysts. Here we have synthesized Pd@PdAg icosahedra and {111} truncated bi-pyramids with only different surface strains between them as electrocatalysts for the ethanol oxidation reaction (EOR). Due to the same exposed facets and compositions of the two electrocatalysts, their EOR performances are mainly determined by the surface strains of PdAg alloys. These two electrocatalysts provide a perfect model to investigate the role of the strain effect in tuning the EOR performance. It is indicated that Pd@PdAg {111} truncated bi-pyramids with a surface strain of 0.3% show better catalytic activity and durability than Pd@PdAg icosahedra with a surface strain of 2.1% including commercial Pd/C. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that the lowered d-band center of 0.3% strained PdAg alloys relative to 2.1% strained ones reduced the adsorption energy of the acetate-evolution key intermediate *CH3CO, thereby promoting the enhancem

In accordance with the result of d-band centers, the adsorption energies of *CH3CO on these three models followed a sequence of ideal Pd (111) < 2.1% strained Pd3Ag (111) < 0.3% strained Pd3Ag (111), suggesting that Pd3Ag (111) planes with a strain of 0.3% are more active than the structure with a strain of 2.1% than Pd (111). As such, Pd@PdAg {111} truncated bi-pyramids show the best catalytic performance towards the EOR. The best EOR performance of Pd@PdAg {111} truncated bi-pyramids can be further understood through electrochemical analysis. Since the adsorbed intermediates *CH3CO can be oxidized by *OH to acetate, the adsorption potential of *OH is rather important to the performance towards the EOR. The CV curves of the two types of Pd@PdAg nanocrystals are shown in Fig. 4a, and the peaks marked by arrows correspond to the adsorption of *OH. As can be seen, the peak potential of Pd@PdAg {111} truncated bi-pyramids was around 0.6 V vs. RHE, which was 0.04 V lower than that of Pd@PdAg icosahedra (0.64 V vs. RHE), indicating easier adsorption of *OH and oxidation of *CH3CO on the surface of Pd@PdAg {111} truncated bi-pyramids. papers.title: Transition Metal High-Entropy Nanozyme: Multi-Site Orbital Coupling Modulated High-Efficiency Peroxidase Mimics.
papers.system: High-entropy nanozymes composed of five transition metals (Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu)
papers.approach: Synthesis of HEA nanoparticles combined with DFT calculations to probe d-orbital coupling and electronic structure; catalytic testing for peroxidase-like activity
papers.findings: Improved d-orbital coupling increases electron density near the Fermi level and shifts the d-band center; this enhances substrate adsorption and electron transfer, leading to catalytic efficiencies comparable to natural enzymes
papers.mechanism: Enhanced multi-site orbital coupling among constituent metals optimizes the adsorption of intermediates and facilitates site-to-site electron transfer

papers.title: Remote Activation of H-H Bonds by Platinum in Dilute Alloy Catalysts.
papers.system: Dilute platinum atoms in Cu nanoparticles supported on SBA-15 silica
papers.approach: In situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy combined with DFT calculations and kinetic experiments in hydrogenation of unsaturated aldehydes
papers.findings: Even when Pt atoms are located at the inner metal-support interface rather than on the surface, they modify the electronic density of distant surface Cu atoms, lowering the activation energy for H2 dissociation and improving selectivity
papers.mechanism: Subsurface Pt atoms induce a remote ligand effect on Cu atoms, altering the density of states and thereby influencing the adsorption and dissociation properties of hydrogen

papers.title: Synergistic effects of mixing and strain in high entropy spinel oxides for oxygen evolution reaction.
papers.system: High-entropy spinel oxides containing five 3d-transition metal cations
papers.approach: Combined theoretical (DFT) and experimental studies using a sol-flame synthesis method to evaluate OER activity
papers.findings: Element mixing induces local strain (contraction/expansion) at active metal–oxygen bonds, yielding a broader distribution of adsorption energies and superior OER activity and durability compared to lower-entropy oxides
papers.mechanism: The interplay of multiple metal cations creates strain effects that tune intermediate adsorption energies at active sites, thereby optimizing the reaction thermodynamics

papers.title: Strain effect in Pd@PdAg twinned nanocrystals towards ethanol oxidation electrocatalysis.
papers.system: Pd@PdAg nanocrystals with controlled surface strain differences (0.3% vs. 2.1%)
papers.approach: Synthesis of two morphologically similar nanocrystals (icosahedra and {111} truncated bi-pyramids) with identical composition but different surface strains; electrochemical testing combined with DFT calculations
papers.findings: Nanocrystals with lower surface strain (0.3%) exhibit better catalytic activity and durability in ethanol oxidation due to a more favorable d-band center shift that weakens the adsorption of poisoning intermediates
papers.mechanism: Surface strain modulates the d-band center position of the alloy, thereby controlling the adsorption energy of key intermediates such as *CH3CO, which influences the catalytic performance

papers.title: Impacts of Metal-Support Interaction on Hydrogen Evolution Reaction of Cobalt-Nitride-Carbide Catalyst.
papers.system: Cobalt-nitride-carbide catalysts with Co nanoparticles encapsulated in nitrogen-doped graphitic carbon nanosheets
papers.approach: Synthesis via an organic–inorganic hybridization method with controlled cobalt precursor concentrations; evaluation of the influence of acid treatment to modulate metal-support interactions (MSI) through electrochemical measurements and impedance spectroscopy
papers.findings: An optimal MSI (as seen in Co-N-C0.025M) leads to moderate hydrogen adsorption energy and enhanced charge transfer, resulting in superior HER kinetics and durability compared to catalysts with too small or too large Co nanoparticle sizes
papers.mechanism: The electron transfer between encapsulated Co nanoparticles and the carbon support, mediated by MSI, facilitates reactant adsorption and optimizes hydrogen evolution reaction kinetics

papers.title: A High-Entropy Single-Atom Catalyst Toward Oxygen Reduction Reaction in Acidic and Alkaline Conditions.
papers.system: Nitrogen-doped graphene-supported high-entropy single-atom catalysts (HESAC) containing Fe, Co, Ni, and Ru
papers.approach: Design guided by DFT and machine learning to predict optimal ORR performance; synthesis and comprehensive spectroscopic characterization followed by performance testing in both acidic and alkaline electrolytes
papers.findings: The synergistic non-bonding effects between multiple metal atoms lower the adsorption energy of OH intermediates on Fe sites, resulting in ORR overpotentials comparable to Pt/C catalysts alongside excellent durability and high kinetic performance
papers.mechanism: Non-bonding interactions among adjacent atomically dispersed metals modulate the electronic structure of active sites (e.g., shifting the d-band center), thereby tuning the adsorption energetics for the key reaction intermediates

papers.title: Hydrogen Evolution Reaction on Ultra-Smooth Sputtered Nanocrystalline Ni Thin Films in Alkaline Media-From Intrinsic Activity to the Effects of Surface Oxidation
papers.system: Ultra-smooth nanocrystalline Ni thin films with controlled surface oxidation (formation of Ni(OH)2)
papers.approach: Fabrication via magnetron sputtering combined with cyclic voltammetry, TEM, XPS, and AFM analysis; supported by DFT and kinetic Monte Carlo simulations
papers.findings: Partial surface oxidation leads predominantly to Ni(OH)2 formation with minimal roughening, resulting in 3–5 times higher HER exchange current densities compared to as-deposited films, although excessive roughening may eventually deteriorate performance
papers.mechanism: The formation of surface hydroxide phases modulates the free energy of hydrogen adsorption, thereby promoting optimal charge transfer kinetics during HER

papers.title: PtFeCoNiCu high-entropy solid solution alloy as highly efficient electrocatalyst for the oxygen reduction reaction.
papers.system: High-entropy alloy nanoparticles consisting of Pt, Fe, Co, Ni, and Cu
papers.approach: Preparation via impregnation reduction method followed by spectroscopic characterization (XPS, XANES) and supported by DFT calculations; performance evaluation in ORR (including fuel cell tests)
papers.findings: The alloy exhibits a marked improvement in ORR mass activity, stability, and power density compared to commercial Pt/C catalysts, credited to a ligand effect that downshifts the d-band center
papers.mechanism: Multi-element alloying induces a ligand effect that optimizes the surface electronic structure, leading to decreased adsorption energy for oxygen species and enhanced activation of the O–O bond

papers.title: Atomically Dispersed Iridium on Indium Tin Oxide Efficiently Catalyzes Water Oxidation.
papers.system: Atomically dispersed Iridium sites on indium tin oxide (ITO) for oxygen evolution reaction
papers.approach: Surface organometallic chemistry synthesis followed by in situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy for tracking reaction intermediates; mechanistic modeling
papers.findings: Under OER conditions, Ir is oxidized to form an IrV=O intermediate that likely serves as the catalyst resting state before further oxidation to IrVI, enabling rapid water nucleophilic attack and oxygen evolution
papers.mechanism: The formation and subsequent oxidation of a high-valent Ir–oxo species (IrV=O to IrVI) control the water oxidation kinetics via a water nucleophilic attack pathway

established: The d-band center position and electronic structure (ligand effect) are crucial determinants of catalytic activity and selectivity.
Metal-support interactions can modulate charge transfer kinetics and intermediate adsorption energies.
Strain engineering in alloy and nanocrystal catalysts effectively alters the adsorption characteristics of key reaction intermediates.
High-entropy materials and single-atom catalysts offer opportunities for creating multiple active sites and enhanced durability.

approaches_tried.approach: High-entropy alloy design and mixing of multiple transition metals
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced catalytic performance (activity, selectivity, durability) across reactions like ORR and OER due to tuned electronic structures and multiple active sites

approaches_tried.approach: Single-atom alloy strategy with dilute dopant (Pt in Cu) and probing metal-support interface effects
approaches_tried.outcome: Remote activation of H–H bonds with improved selectivity observed, despite dopants being located subsurface

approaches_tried.approach: Strain engineering via controlled synthesis of nanocrystals
approaches_tried.outcome: Optimized surface strain leads to favorable adsorption energies for reaction intermediates, improving ethanol oxidation kinetics

approaches_tried.approach: Controlled surface oxidation and modulation of metal-support interactions
approaches_tried.outcome: Formation of surface hydroxide phases and optimized MSI enhance the HER performance of Ni and Co-based catalysts

mechanisms: d-band center shifts (via ligand effects, strain, or alloying) govern the adsorption and activation energies of intermediates
Remote electronic modulation from subsurface dopants influences the reactivity of surface atoms
Metal-support interactions facilitate charge transfer and control the optimal binding of species
Formation of high-valent metal–oxo or hydroxide intermediates drives the catalytic cycles in oxidation and reduction reactions
disagreements: Whether dopant atoms in single-atom alloy systems act as electronically isolated centers or interact with the host metal over several lattice distances
The precise interplay and decoupling of contributions from strain, ligand effects, and metal-support interactions in determining activity
open_questions: How to quantitatively decouple the individual contributions of strain, alloying, and metal-support interactions on catalytic performance under varying reaction conditions
The long-term stability and structural evolution of catalysts under operando conditions and its direct correlation with mechanistic pathways
Boundaries within which each mechanism (e.g., remote activation vs. surface activation) dominates the reactivity for different reactions and electrolytes
opportunities: Design controlled comparisons where catalysts with identical compositions are synthesized with varying degrees of surface strain or MSI, to isolate their effects
Employ in situ spectroscopic techniques to monitor electronic structure changes induced by subsurface dopants under reactive conditions
Combine high-entropy material design with strain engineering to access novel multi-active sites for improved durability and selectivity in electrocatalysis
Utilize machine learning alongside DFT to predict optimal combinations and configurations that balance ligand effects, strain, and metal-support interactions

directions.assessment: Using high-entropy alloy catalysts can tune the distribution of active sites and electronic structure (i.e. d-band center shifts) by mixing multiple transition metals. This approach directly targets activity and durability but can sometimes blur the role of individual effects due to compositional complexity. It is supported by DFT and experimental studies (e.g., PMC10667809 and PMC9860490) though the exact contributions of each metal can be hard to decouple.

Modulating the surface strain via synthesis controls the d-band center and hence the binding energy of adsorbates. This direction directly addresses how catalytic activity and selectivity are governed, as shown in Pd@PdAg systems (PMC9419203). The physics is well established through d-band theory and is highly feasible using controlled synthesis methods that yield nanocrystals with identical composition but different strain states.

Altering the extent of metal–support interaction (e.g., via acid treatments or controlled encapsulation) can affect electron transfer and intermediate adsorption, thereby influencing HER and other reactions. Evidence from Co-N-C catalysts (PMC8844497) supports this, but isolating MSI effects from other structural parameters can be challenging.

directions.direction: Remote Electronic Activation via Subsurface Dopants
directions.assessment: Embedding catalytically active dopant atoms beneath the surface (as in dilute alloys) can remotely tailor surface electronic properties. This mechanism (as in Pt-doped Cu systems, PMC11075014) offers an interesting approach but may be less direct in establishing structure–activity relationships because the dopant is not at the surface.

directions.direction: In Situ Mechanistic Characterization of Reaction Intermediates
directions.assessment: Using in situ spectroscopic techniques to directly observe adsorbed intermediates (e.g., metal–oxo or hydroxide species) during reactions can help decouple electronic effects (e.g., ligand, strain, MSI) on catalyst performance. Such studies provide rich mechanistic insights but require sophisticated instrumentation and data interpretation.

choice.why: This approach directly modulates the catalyst’s electronic structure by controlling the d-band center via surface strain. Studies on Pd@PdAg nanocrystals show that lowering surface strain (from ~2.1% to ~0.3%) shifts the d-band center downward, weakening adsorbate binding and improving catalytic selectivity and durability. The physics is well understood, and controlled synthesis to obtain identical compositions with different strain levels is achievable, making it highly informative and feasible for a strong research group.
